text:
The Social Housing Bill was introduced into the House of Lords in May 2026 and has now progressed to the Commons.

The bill brings forward comprehensive reforms that safeguard existing social housing while supporting the sector to increase future supply. It recalibrates the Right to Buy scheme to preserve a route to home ownership for longstanding tenants while better protecting stock and ensuring more homes are built than lost, including through changes to eligibility, discounts and exemptions for new homes. The bill also introduces a new requirement on private registered providers of social housing to notify the council and other providers before selling social homes, maximising opportunities to retain them.

The bill also strengthens protections for social tenants experiencing domestic abuse, enabling joint tenant survivors to remain in their property away from their abuser or move to suitable alternative accommodation. Finally, by repealing unworkable legacy provisions from previous housing legislation and streamlining the housing consents process for councils, the bill will clarify the statute book and reduce unnecessary bureaucracy, helping to enable sustained investment in social and affordable housing.

The government is introducing a package of amendments to the bill at Commons Committee stage, which looks to strengthen protections for social housing tenants, deliver on the government’s commitments to tackle homelessness, and bolster the bill’s provisions to protect social housing stock.

This guide explains the individual amendments being made and the intentions behind these changes.

Protection of existing social housing stock

Strengthening the disposals notification requirement

Following further engagement with the sector and parliamentarians, the government is looking to further strengthen the disposals notification requirement in the bill, to ensure we maximise opportunities for social homes to stay within the regulated sector. This includes:

extending the notification period from 4 to 8 weeks. There will now be a an 8-week period after the notification has taken place before the sale of a property outside of the regulated sector can be completed. This will give local authorities and other registered providers more time to consider a possible purchase. The 8-week time period aims to strike an effective balance between allowing potential buyers more time for consideration, whilst avoiding prolonged delays to sales for private registered providers. During the notification period, providers will remain free to market properties, engage with potential buyers and progress disposal plans in the usual way

including additional property information in notification. When providing a notification about the intention to sell a social home out of the regulated sector, private registered providers will be required to include information about the type of rent the home was previously let at, given that this will directly influence the level of rent that a purchasing registered provider could charge. This will help to inform decisions for those considering purchasing the home, further maximising opportunities to retain homes within the social housing sector

Right to Buy rural self-designation

The bill’s comprehensive package of reforms includes an exemption from the Right to Buy for social housing in rural areas. This is in recognition of the unique challenges of replacing social and affordable homes in rural areas, including land, planning and supply constraints.

Following debate in the Lords, the government is bringing forward an amendment that will give councils more control to protect affordable homes in rural communities. This includes allowing councils to designate eligible rural areas themselves where they meet the rural criteria, in order to exempt them from Right to Buy. Currently, councils have to apply for designation from the Secretary of State, and moving to self-designation will reduce bureaucracy for both councils and the government.

The government will set out in regulations the criteria for rural areas and the process for self-designation. The long-established criteria – that areas should have a population density of no more than 2 persons per hectare and a population of 3,000 or fewer – will remain in place.

Greater protections for social housing tenants

Strengthening the domestic abuse tenancy reform measures

During passage through the Lords, the government broadened the bill’s domestic abuse protections to include victims of familial abuse in non-partnership relationships and to align the bill’s provisions more closely with the Domestic Abuse Act 2021.

The government is now bringing forward amendments to further strengthen these protections. This includes:

bolstering the discretionary possession grounds. The amendment will mean that the existence of a relevant protective order(a Domestic Abuse Protection Order or a Non-Molestation Order) will be sufficient for the court to determine whether it is reasonable to make a possession order. This change will help streamline and accelerate the process, and give greater confidence to landlords and victims when seeking possession

clarifying the operation of the tenancy transfer mechanism. The bill already includes a new mechanism to facilitate the transfer of the joint tenancy into the sole name of the victim, where a victim wants to remain in the home as a sole tenant. The bill also includes powers to enable the courts to make an order to provide the victim with suitable alternative accommodation, where it is not appropriate for the victim to remain in a home and the landlord has this accommodation available. The amendments being made to the bill will ensure that where the court makes an order either on the basis that the victim remains in the home as sole tenant or on the basis that they are to be provided with suitable alternative accommodation, then the perpetrator’s interest in the joint tenancy will be brought to an end

minor and technical amendments. These amendments are to ensure the bill’s provisions operate as intended, enabling the legislation to be applied consistently across different tenancy regimes and aligned with adjacent legislation including the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 and the Housing Acts 1985 and 1988

Right to Manage reforms

The Right to Manage (RTM) gives local authority tenants a statutory route to take on responsibility for managing housing services through a Tenant Management Organisation (TMO). The government’s response to the Grenfell Tower Inquiry, published in 2025, committed to reviewing oversight arrangements for delegated management organisations, including TMOs.

The review found that the RTM remains an important route for resident control, but that take-up has declined and existing TMOs face growing pressures. Most TMOs are small organisations with limited staffing and volunteer capacity. Stakeholders reported that the set-up process can be complex, access to advice and training is limited, and governance requirements do not always reflect the size, capacity and functions of individual TMOs.

The review also found that roles and responsibilities between TMOs and landlords are not always clear. Management agreements can be outdated and may not reflect current consumer regulation or building safety requirements. Information sharing and performance monitoring are inconsistent, while allowance calculations can be difficult to understand and may not fully reflect rising compliance costs.

The government is therefore bringing forwards amendments to modernise the framework, make it easier for social housing residents to take control of their housing services, and strengthen oversight and accountability. This includes:

broadening regulation-making powers, which will enable clearer and more consistent requirements to be set on matters relating to the ongoing operation of TMOs as well as their setup; these requirements will relate to governance, information sharing, financial management and regulatory compliance

establishing mandatory core requirements on information sharing, ballot arrangements, and conducting reviews, which will be added to existing management agreements. These requirements will bring greater clarity to the respective responsibilities of TMO and local authorities, and consistency with current regulatory requirements, including for building safety and social housing consumer regulations

enabling a tiered governance model to be introduced through regulations. This will ensure that governance, assurance and oversight requirements are proportionate to the scale, complexity and risk of the functions a TMO manages

creating a court-backed intervention route for serious failures. Courts will be able to remove officers, transfer functions, or terminate agreements where necessary and proportionate. This will act as a safeguard of last resort in exceptional cases involving serious governance failures, misconduct or risks to residents’ safety

Tackling homelessness

Duty of private registered provider to offer accommodation after local authority request (Duty to Offer)

In the National Plan to End Homelessness (December 2025), the government committed to considering levers to require social housing landlords to rehouse statutory homeless households referred by the council, where joint working is not operating effectively, including legislating if necessary.

To deliver on this commitment, the government is bringing forward an amendment that will introduce a new statutory power. This power will enable a local housing authority (LHA) to refer a homeless household (owed the main housing duty) to a private registered provider of social housing (PRP), requiring the PRP to offer suitable accommodation to that household, unless they have good reason not to. This measure is designed to strengthen cooperation between LHAs and PRPs and ensure social housing is used effectively to prevent homelessness.

The Secretary of State will set out through regulations what constitutes a reasonable period for making an offer and the circumstances in which a PRP may be regarded as having a good reason not to offer accommodation. We will work with stakeholders to develop these regulations.

Duties of specified bodies to collaborate and act on homelessness

The National Plan to End Homelessness includes a commitment to legislate for a ‘Duty to Collaborate’, to compel public services to work together to prevent homelessness and support those who are at crisis point. The government is delivering on this commitment by introducing several new duties for specified bodies in relation to homelessness.

These new duties build on and will replace the existing Duty to Refer by requiring specified bodies to take proactive steps, as part of their normal functions, to identify those who are homeless, or at risk of homelessness. They require those bodies to assess their needs, and work together with other organisations such as local authorities, taking coordinated action to prevent homelessness and address it as early as possible.

Targeted engagement has taken place with the homelessness sector, including our Homelessness Expert Group, alongside other government departments and some local authorities, to inform the development of these new duties, which are:

a duty that specified bodies must identify actual or possible homelessness. Specified bodies will be required – as part of their usual functions – to identify at the earliest opportunity those who are homeless, threatened with homelessness, or otherwise at risk of homelessness

a duty that specified bodies must act on actual or possible homelessness. When a specified body identifies a person is homeless or at risk of homelessness, they will be required to notify a local housing authority (the ‘duty to notify the local housing authority’). They will be required to ask the person if they have already made an application for support to a local authority and seek their consent to do so if they haven’t

a general duty to act. Once a specified body has identified that a person is homeless or at risk of homelessness, they will be required to take appropriate action, consistent with its normal functions to prevent or reduce the risk of homelessness, or to relieve it or alleviate its impact. This also includes a requirement to consult other bodies or services where reasonable to do so, to ensure a holistic approach to homelessness. The specified body must also engage with the local housing authority, to enable it to assist the individual (the ‘duty to engage with local housing authorities’)

delegated powers. A regulation making power is included so that bodies can be specified in secondary legislation, and so the list of bodies can be updated to add, remove or amend bodies who are subject to the new duty. A regulation making power is also included to define in secondary legislation how specified bodies can or must comply with their duties to (a) identify homelessness; (b) notify the local housing authority; (c) exercise the general duty to act and (d) engage with local housing authorities

Veterans: power to exempt from local connection referrals for homelessness assistance

The government is also taking action to reduce potential barriers to receiving support for veterans facing homelessness. This amendment allows the government to specify circumstances in which a local housing authority may not refer a case to another authority.

The government intends to use this provision to ensure that if a veteran presents to any local authority in England for homelessness assistance, the receiving authority will not be able to refer them elsewhere, regardless of whether the veteran has a connection to a different authority. This will ultimately ensure that veterans receive timely support when seeking homelessness assistance from a local authority.
